intro_en:
This segment of the Israel National Trail begins in Nahal Havah, passes the Havah pools (gvim) and climbs through the "Cracks" (HaSdakim) - a beautiful tributary of Nahal Havah with unique rock-weathering formations. Further along the route we reach the rim of Makhtesh Ramon, with fine views over the crater's landscapes on its eastern side.

 Hod Akev - Nahal Havah (41)
 Mitzpe Ramon - Nahal Gevanim (43)
character_en: In Nahal Havah there is a short stretch of climbing. Most of the segment follows an easy walking route on dirt tracks
shortcuts_en: It is possible to shorten the segment and finish the walk at Ma'ale Mahmal in Makhtesh Ramon
transport_en: At the southern end point in Mitzpe Ramon
pois_en: The Havah pools. The Sdakim channel. Lookouts over Makhtesh Ramon. Environmental sculpture in Mitzpe Ramon
important_en: Reaching the overnight campsite above Nahal Havah, where the segment begins from the north, is possible only with an off-road vehicle.
A long day of walking; it is advisable to start walking early.

It is possible to shorten the route and descend into Makhtesh Ramon via Ma'ale Mahmal, with a pre-arranged vehicle pick-up from the foot of the ascent (before dark, in accordance with the traffic rules in nature reserves).
description_en:
We set out from the overnight campsite above Nahal Havah and head along the Oil Road with black marking. Further on, the Israel National Trail descends into the channel of Nahal Havah. We turn left with the blue marking.
After a short walk, before the stream reaches a waterfall and enters a canyon, the trail climbs onto the southern bank, continues above the canyon and after a few minutes' walk descends back into the channel.
Before continuing with the Israel National Trail down Nahal Havah, it is worth going back a short distance up the channel with the black marking, into the narrow canyon, to visit the Havah pools and the waterfall. Before the waterfall, a large boulder is wedged between the canyon walls above a large rock pool that holds water all year round. Caper bushes and wild fig trees grow inside the canyon and on its walls.
Those who detoured from the trail to the pools return to the Israel National Trail. After a short walk, the trail curves right with the channel, and a dark rock is exposed in the channel - flint from the Senonian age.
Before the main channel of the stream curves left, the Israel National Trail turns right with the green marking.
Those who wish can again leave the Israel National Trail and walk down the channel to Ein Havah - a beautiful spring whose water drips from the wall of a waterfall into a small pool (a quarter of an hour's walk each way).
From this point, the trail climbs up a tributary of Nahal Havah - which looks innocent at its entrance, but the further we go into it, the more surprising the sights it offers. It has large boulders that have collapsed into it, a sloping surface of flint, rock masses in a host of sculpted shapes, and the climax - the trail enters a narrow crack between rock walls and climbs through it to the back of the ridge. Here the expanses of the Avdat Plateau open up before us.
The clear line of the trail has been trodden by the feet of many hikers. After a stretch of walking, the dirt track of the Oil Road comes into view on the right. We walk parallel to the Oil Road and reach a junction with a red-marked track coming from the left, from the direction of Ma'ale Noah. After a short distance we meet the Oil Road itself, and continue along it south with the black marking.
After a few minutes' walk, a green footpath leaves the Oil Road to the left towards Ma'ale Mahmal. If you have chosen to shorten the segment and finish the walk at the foot of Ma'ale Mahmal inside Makhtesh Ramon, turn left towards Metzad Mahmal and Ma'ale Mahmal.
Those continuing to Mitzpe Ramon can also leave the Israel National Trail here and follow the green marking. This is an opportunity to see the remains of a historic rainwater storage pool, an ancient predator trap beside the track and a fine view over Makhtesh Ramon from Metzad Mahmal - an ancient fort that controlled the exit of the Incense Route from the crater at the top of Ma'ale Mahmal. To return to the Israel National Trail from the fort, go back along the same green-marked route you came by, an addition of about half a km of walking each way.
The track and the trail curve slightly right and after a few minutes, when an electricity pylon of a power line comes into view ahead, we reach a junction of tracks: the Israel National Trail turns right with the black marking, and the Oil Road turns left towards the wall of Makhtesh Ramon. Here nature and the landscape paid a heavy price for the Eilat-Ashkelon oil pipeline project: running the pipeline through the crater wall on both sides, in the north of the crater at Ma'ale Mahmal and opposite in the south near Mount Saharonim, damaged the landscape and left prominent scars. (You are welcome to read here about SPNI's struggle against the present-day environmental dangers of the oil pipeline.)
The Israel National Trail continues along the dirt track, and together with it moves away from the crater rim on a wide curve. Don't worry - further along the way we return to the crater rim for a stretch of walking with fine views.
All at once the vast Makhtesh Ramon appears in all its glory. Further along the way it is worth pausing at the Givat Ga'ash lookout, for a view over the crater and especially its north-eastern part. The crater is a history book of ancient geology. The excavation deep into the earth's crust reveals evidence of geological events that occurred in ancient eras. One of these is an ancient volcano called Givat Ga'ash (Volcano Hill), which can be seen below us. It is a dark hill with the shape of a crater still discernible at its centre. Further off to the left we see the "nose" of Mount Ardon. Mount Ardon divides the eastern wing of the crater into two valleys: the one we see at its foot - the Mahmal Valley - and the Ardon Valley, which lies on the other side of Mount Ardon and which we will look out over again further along the trail, when we walk along the crater's edge on its other side, on the Harirrim ridge.
Note the cracks in the rocks around the viewing terrace. The formation of the crater continues all the time. The forces of weathering undermine the foundations, the soft layers deep in the crater are washed away, and the hard limestone layers above them crack and collapse into the crater in a slow but continuous process, even in our own day.
The way to Mitzpe Ramon is getting long, but "maybe we'll still manage to kill a small Turk of an evening in Mitzpe Ramon", as Meir Ariel and David Broza sang in the song "Be'Tzohorei HaYom" (At Midday). As we approach Mitzpe Ramon, we first see the houses of the town on the horizon, then the trail passes through environmental sculptures, and also beside a grove with KKL-JNF picnic tables and a water tap. The segment ends at the petrol station at the entrance to Mitzpe Ramon.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, trail-marking coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
